content: The film Unnecessary Fuss was produced by Ingrid Newkirk and Alex Pacheco of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA). It contains footage recorded inside the University of Pennsylvania's Head Injury Clinic in Philadelphia during 1983-1984. The footage, captured by the researchers themselves, documents experiments in which brain injuries were inflicted on baboons using a hydraulic device. These experiments were part of a research project aimed at studying head injuries caused by vehicle and sports accidents. The video shows researchers laughing as the brain damage was inflicted on the animals. In May 1984, the Animal Liberation Front (ALF) raided the laboratory and removed 60 hours of audio and video recordings. They handed the material over to PETA, which edited it into a 26-minute film with voice-over commentary by Newkirk. The film was distributed to the media and Congress, leading to significant public backlash. As a result, the laboratory was shut down, the chief veterinarian was fired, and the university was placed on probation. The title Unnecessary Fuss originates from a statement made by Dr. Thomas Gennarelli, the head of the clinic, in 1983. He declined to describe his research to a newspaper, stating that it had the potential to stir up all sorts of unnecessary fuss. The film depicts at least one sedated but not anesthetized baboon restrained on an operating table. The animal's shaved head was secured inside a helmet using dental cement. A hydraulic device, known as Penn 2, struck the baboon's head from behind, simulating whiplash by pushing the head forward at a 60-degree angle with a force reportedly up to 1,000 g. After the injury, the baboon's head was removed from the helmet using a hammer and screwdriver. In one sequence, part of the baboon's ear was torn off along with the helmet. A researcher is heard laughing and saying, It's a boy, followed by, Looks like I left a little ear behind. The footage also shows researchers laughing at injured baboons, performing electrocautery on a seemingly conscious baboon, smoking cigarettes and pipes during surgery, and playing loud music while the animals were being injured. In one scene, a severely injured baboon is held up to the camera while researchers mockingly speak to the animal, followed by laughter. Another sequence shows a brain-damaged, drooling monkey strapped into a high chair in the corner of the room, with a researcher making sarcastic comments about the animal's condition. The University of Pennsylvania responded to the film by calling it a caricature of what had occurred in the laboratory. Before PETA released the footage, Dr. Thomas Langfitt, the chief investigator at the Head Injury Clinic, denied any abuse in the lab. He stated that the animals were treated humanely and that researchers would never laugh at the apes, claiming, We treat the baboons the way we treat human beings. An investigation by 18 veterinarians from the American College of Laboratory Animal Medicine, commissioned by the Office for Protection from Research Risks (OPRR), concluded that the PETA film had grossly overstated the deficiencies in the Head Injury Clinic. However, after a three-day sit-in by animal rights activists at the National Institutes for Health and intervention by Margaret Heckler, then Secretary of Health and Human Services, the government determined that the extraordinarily serious violations seen in the footage justified the clinic's closure. These violations included questionable depth of anesthetic coma, lack of veterinary oversight before and after surgery, failure to maintain aseptic surgical techniques, improper cleaning of the operating theater, and smoking in the operating room despite the presence of oxygen tanks. The OPRR also identified deficiencies in other laboratories operated by the university. The university's chief veterinarian was fired, new training programs were implemented, and the university was placed on probation, requiring quarterly progress reports to the OPRR. When PETA released its 26-minute film, the OPRR initially refused to investigate because the footage had been edited from 60 hours of videotape. PETA withheld the unedited material for over a year before eventually releasing it. Upon review, the OPRR found that the brain damage depicted in the film involved only one baboon out of the 150 subjected to the Penn 2 injuries. The film gave the impression that multiple animals were involved in the brain-damage scenes. The OPRR also identified 25 errors in Newkirk's voice-over commentary, including a misrepresentation of an accidental water spill on a conscious baboon during surgery as an acid spill.
